## Industry Problem

<!--
  instructor: Don't open with the code. Open with the stakes: ask "what's
  the worst thing that happens if this agent is wrong?" for a retail tool
  (1_2) vs. this one. The gap in acceptable failure cost is the whole reason
  1.5.1 exists as its own competency instead of just being "more testing."
-->

A clinical intake agent reviews a patient's symptoms and decides to schedule a follow-up appointment with a specialist. If it's wrong — wrong specialist, wrong urgency, or wrong patient entirely — a real person's care is affected. Unlike the retail or telecom tools you've built so far, this is not a case where you can just fix it next release.

## Instructor Example / Demonstration

<!--
  instructor: Live-run this and actually trigger the interrupt in front of
  the class — don't just show the code. Pause on the printed interrupt
  object and ask "what information would a nurse reviewing this need to see
  right now?" before revealing the Command(resume=...) call. Prereq: none
  beyond 1_1's setup; checkpointer is new but self-contained.
-->

Here's the fix: put a human approval gate in front of the tool, using LangChain's `HumanInTheLoopMiddleware`.

```python
from langchain.agents import create_agent
from langchain.agents.middleware import HumanInTheLoopMiddleware
from langgraph.checkpoint.memory import InMemorySaver
from langchain.tools import tool

@tool
def schedule_followup(patient_id: str, specialist: str, urgency: str) -> str:
    """Schedule a follow-up appointment with a specialist for a patient."""
    return f"Scheduled: patient {patient_id} with {specialist} ({urgency} priority)"

agent = create_agent(
    model="google_genai:gemini-2.5-flash",
    tools=[schedule_followup],
    middleware=[
        HumanInTheLoopMiddleware(
            interrupt_on={
                "schedule_followup": {"allowed_decisions": ["approve", "edit", "reject"]},
            },
            description_prefix="Clinical action pending review",
        ),
    ],
    checkpointer=InMemorySaver(),
)
```

Watch what happens on `invoke` — execution pauses *before* the tool runs, and nothing happens until a human decides:

```python
config = {"configurable": {"thread_id": "patient-482-visit"}}

result = agent.invoke(
    {"messages": [{"role": "user", "content": "Patient reports chest pain, schedule urgent cardiology follow-up."}]},
    config=config,
)
print(result.interrupts)  # the proposed action, waiting for a human
```

```python
from langgraph.types import Command

# A human reviews result.interrupts and approves it as-is
final = agent.invoke(Command(resume=[{"type": "approve"}]), config=config)
print(final["messages"][-1].content)
```

## Run It Yourself

<!--
  instructor: ~10 min. Most common snag: forgetting the `config` (thread_id)
  on the resume call — without it the graph has no paused state to resume,
  and the error is confusing. Have them print `result.interrupts` before
  writing any resume logic so they see the actual shape of what a reviewer
  would see.
-->

Run the snippet above yourself. Then try a `reject` decision instead of `approve`, and read what comes back — notice the agent gets the rejection as feedback, not just a silent failure.

## Modify It, Build It

<!--
  instructor: ~15 min, pairs. Good work looks like a clear, deliberate
  choice about which decisions are allowed on which tool, and a spoken
  justification for it. The `when` predicate is the stretch goal — don't
  require it, but flag it as the "smart" version of this pattern.
-->

Add a second tool — sending a message to the patient's care team, say — and give it a *different* `allowed_decisions` set than `schedule_followup` (e.g. no `edit`, only `approve`/`reject`). Be ready to justify why that tool deserves stricter or looser review than the first. (Stretch: add a `when` predicate so only high-urgency calls interrupt.)

## Apply It

<!--
  instructor: Flag explicitly that any tool with a real-world side effect
  (sending a message, booking something, moving money) in the Unit 1
  personal-assistant project needs this pattern, not just healthcare tools —
  this is a general guardrail requirement, and a strong Pass-off candidate

-->

Add a human-approval gate to any action-taking tool in your Unit 1 personal-assistant project — anything that sends, books, or changes something in the real world, not just this healthcare example.
